awd_titl_txt: PRIMES: Integration of Mathematical Research and Learning for high school students
awd_abstract_narration:
PRIMES (Program for Research in Mathematics, Engineering and Science) will select talented high school students from across the U.S. via rigorous testing. Under the guidance of academic mentors, program participants will conduct year-long research projects, write papers, and make conference presentations. Groups of students will also participate in guided reading, online research forums, and a residential summer math camp. The program will create a pipeline of mathematical talent and support graduate students and undergraduates serving as mentors.

Topics for student research projects will include ancient ALE Ricci flows and dynamical energy functionals, refractive outer billiards, fields of definition of abelian surfaces of maximal Picard rank, semisimplifications of representations of gl(n), Temperley-Lieb algebras and canonical bases, tournament and digraph inversions, machine learning for physical systems, sparse inference of earthquake dynamics, and Fresnel inversion and the NASA Cassini Mission. More details and information about the program may be found on the PRIMES website: https://math.mit.edu/research/highschool/primes.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Award Title: PRIMES: Integration of Mathematical Research and Learning for High School Students

Federal Award ID: DMS-2522789

 

PRIMES is a free mathematical research and enrichment program for high school students, created in the MIT Mathematics Department in October 2010. It includes several sections: MIT PRIMES offers year-long research projects in mathematics and bioinformatics to students from Greater Boston; PRIMES-USA is a national math research program for high school juniors and sophomores; PRIMES Circle is a math enrichment section for high school students from the Boston area; MathROOTS is a two-week math enrichment residential summer program for nationally selected high-potential high school students; and CrowdMath is a massive online collaborative year-long research project open to all high school and college students around the world.

 

PRIMES gives talented high school students a unique opportunity to experience the joy and beauty of mathematical research, inspires them to pursue careers in the mathematical sciences, and helps diversify the pool of students interested in mathematics by providing opportunities for young women and underrepresented groups.

 

In 2025-2026, 202 high school students participated in mathematical research and reading under the guidance of their academic mentors. They authored 41 research papers, gave presentations at two conferences, and won 34 awards at national and international science competitions.

 

PRIMES has developed an innovative approach, based on the combination of learning and research, which allows high school students to learn advanced areas of math and science and to participate in cutting-edge research in a short period of time. Projects are formulated by university faculty and mentored by graduate students and postdoctoral scholars. MIT PRIMES has provided an innovative, year-long model for guiding high school student research. PRIMES-USA has developed techniques for remote mentoring via video teleconferencing. PRIMES Circle has developed an engaging math enrichment curriculum for promising mathematics students. MathROOTS has developed an innovative curriculum of creating problem-solving and a set of social activities for integrating students into campus life. CrowdMath has adapted the Polymath model for high school research mentoring in the open online forum format.

 

PRIMES has developed a set of guidelines for formulating successful mathematical projects for high school research:

 

1. Accessible beginning. The initial steps must be simple to get started.

 

2. Flexibility. It is useful to think about several related questions, switching from one to another if stuck, and to tweak the questions if they are too hard or insufficiently interesting.

 

3. Computer (experimental) component. The possibility of computer-assisted exploration aimed at finding patterns and making conjectures is very useful. In this case, students, who often have strong programming skills, can contribute to the project early, even when they don’t yet have a working knowledge of theoretical tools. It is also easier to learn new mathematical concepts, e.g., those from algebra and representation theory, through hands-on experience with a computer algebra system.

 

4. Advisor involvement. It is important to have an opportunity to consult with a research mathematician other than the mentor – usually the professor or researcher who suggested the project.

 

5. Big picture/motivation. It is important to connect, at least at the level of ideas, to a wider context and to other people’s work.

 

6. Learning component. The project should encourage the students to study advanced mathematics on a regular basis.

 

7. Feasibility. It would be reasonable to expect that a good student would obtain some new results within several months and produce publishable results in one year.

 

8. Relation to the mentor’s research program or area.

 

The results of PRIMES research have been widely disseminated at conferences, posted online for free access, and submitted to academic journals for publication.

 

PRIMES has explored various formats of research and enrichments activities, such as individual and group research projects, guided reading group, distance mentoring over telecommunication channels, studying advanced topics in a game-like setting, writing of research and expository papers, and conference presentations. The experience of running the PRIMES program has been summed up in an article by PI Pavel Etingof and two members of PRIMES staff, Slava Gerovitch and Tanya Khovanova, “Mathematical Research in High School: The PRIMES Experience,” published in The Notices of the American Mathematical Society 62 (2015). The experience of CrowdMath has been shared in a joint article by Etingof, Gerovitch, and CrowdMath mentor Jesse Geneson in the collection, Expanding Undergraduate Research in Mathematics, edited by M. Dorff, J. Rychtář, and D. Taylor (MAA, 2023). PRIMES has established partnerships with a number of other universities. The dissemination of the PRIMES experience should encourage the creation of similar programs at other academic institutions.
